16 Horsepower.summary: Denver band whose Chemnitzer-concertina, hellfire vocals and old-time Appalachian gospel over post-punk intensity founded the gothic-country subgenre.

20/20.summary: Tulsa-to-LA power-pop band whose tightly written, ringing-guitar debut sat with the Knack and the Records at the polished, new-wave end of the genre.

22\u00ba Halo.summary: Philadelphia songwriter Will Kennedy's project blending folk, slacker rock and bedroom pop into hopeful, plainspoken songs written through hardship.

28th Day.summary: Short-lived Chico, California jangle-pop trio, with a young Barbara Manning on bass, whose lone ringing, melancholy EP was produced by True West's Russ Tolman.

2nd Grade.summary: Peter Gill's Philadelphia project crams Guided by Voices- and Big Star-indebted hooks into prolific, miniature-song power-pop sprawls.
2nd Grade.related: Friendship; Hour; Hurry; Golden Apples; Lawn

49 Winchester.summary: Southwest Virginia band whose plainspoken, Appalachian arena-Americana splits the difference between The Band's groove and Tyler Childers's directness.
49 Winchester.related: Tyler Childers; Zach Bryan; Chris Stapleton

764-HERO.summary: Seattle Up Records band whose ringing, unhurried guitar interplay and plainspoken vocals made them a quieter cousin of tourmates Modest Mouse.

Abbey Blackwell.summary: Seattle bassist-turned-songwriter whose rich, lush-voiced, organically arranged folk records grew steadily more confident across a self-released run.

Abel.summary: Columbus songwriter whose self-lacerating, ramshackle country-jangle debut fits the small-label DIY twang network of Julia's War and Candlepin.

Acetone.summary: Los Angeles trio whose slow, country-tinged, hushed-vocal drone shared Vernon Yard Records with early Low, working a hazy desert-highway strain of slowcore.

Ada Lea.summary: Montreal songwriter Alexandra Levy who traded moody indie rock for breezy, Dylan-referencing '70s Laurel Canyon folk warmth.

Adam Faucett.summary: Little Rock songwriter whose weathered, cracked baritone and sparse arrangements deepened into fuller, bleaker band records on Last Chance Records.

Adeline Hotel.summary: Dan Knishkowy's gentle, fingerpicked indie-folk project of plainspoken, wry songs about memory, part of a close-knit Brooklyn songwriter circle.
Adeline Hotel.related: Frank Meadows; Jackie West; The Bird Calls

Adrianne Lenker.summary: Big Thief singer whose parallel solo catalog runs from embryonic teenage recordings to hushed, cabin-recorded confessionals and a Grammy-nominated late high point.
Adrianne Lenker.related: Big Thief; Buck Meek; Gillian Welch

Adrianne Lenker & Buck Meek.summary: A pre-Big Thief duo release of stripped-back, harmony-driven folk documenting the songwriting chemistry between Lenker and Meek.
Adrianne Lenker & Buck Meek.related: Big Thief; Adrianne Lenker; Buck Meek

Advance Base.summary: Owen Ashworth's post-Casiotone project sets deadpan, plainly sung short stories over minimal drum machine and synth, continuing the Drag City deadpan school.
Advance Base.related: Casiotone for the Painfully Alone; Silver Jews

Age of Peace.summary: Los Angeles duo Angie Willcutt and Micah Wu's spectral, folk-based Cosmic American Music, plucked strings and mallet pulse under playful, transcendental lyrics.

Alan Jackson.summary: Georgia neotraditionalist whose plain drawl and fiddle-and-steel arrangements defended honky-tonk country as Music Row turned pop.

Alasdair Roberts.summary: Glasgow songwriter whose spare, fingerpicked solo work after Appendix Out steeps Scottish and Appalachian folk phrasing in the Drag City deadpan-folk lineage.

Alejandro Escovedo.summary: Austin songwriter who moved from punk and cowpunk bands into orchestral, string-laden chamber-rock Americana about grief and Texas-Mexican family history.
Alejandro Escovedo.related: the Nuns; Rank and File; True Believers

Alela Diane.summary: Nevada City folk singer whose clear, unadorned voice carries home-recorded, hymn-and-ballad-rooted songwriting into fuller, then quieter and more domestic, records.

Alela Diane & Wild Divine.summary: Alela Diane credited jointly with her touring band on a warmer, full-band folk-rock record built around her marriage to guitarist Tom Bevitori.

Alex Chilton.summary: Post-Big Star Memphis songwriter who turned from polished jangle to deliberately wrecked, sloppy garage rock and loose, soul-inflected bar-band records.

Alex G.summary: Philadelphia bedroom-pop songwriter whose warped, pitch-shifted vocals and plainspoken menace-and-gentleness grew from prolific Bandcamp lo-fi into major-label pop songcraft.

Alison Krauss & Union Station.summary: Crystalline-voiced, radio-ready bluegrass ensemble whose polished, vocal-forward picking made them the genre's mainstream-crossover face just before O Brother, Where Art Thou?.

Allegra Krieger.summary: New York songwriter whose plainspoken, mortality-fixated diaristic songwriting grew from spare Northern Spy records into a quietly contemplative career high point.

Amalgamated Sons of Rest.summary: One-off unplugged folk-balladry side project pairing Jason Molina with Will Oldham and Alasdair Roberts in close, unpolished front-porch harmonies.
Amalgamated Sons of Rest.related: Jason Molina; Will Oldham; Alasdair Roberts

Amanda Shires.summary: Nashville fiddle player turned literate singer-songwriter whose image-heavy Americana records grew darker and more personal across motherhood and marriage.

Amen Dunes.summary: Damon McMahon's project moved from lo-fi murk into hazy, Dead-and-Parsons-adjacent guitar-folk and then a warmer, radio-scaled classic-rock-informed sound.

American Aquarium.summary: BJ Barham's Raleigh band turned van-touring poverty and later sobriety into plainspoken, conversational Drive-By Truckers- and Lucero-indebted storytelling rock.
American Aquarium.related: Drive-By Truckers; Lucero; Two Cow Garage

American Football.summary: Mike Kinsella's post-Cap'n Jazz project distilled Midwest emo into gentle, jazzy guitar interplay and conversational vocals on its genre-defining lone original album.

American Music Club.summary: San Francisco band led by Mark Eitzel's ragged, plainspoken baritone through slow, pedal-steel-streaked, theatrically bleak country-rock and sadcore songwriting.

Andrew Combs.summary: Nashville songwriter whose warm, classic-leaning country-folk records, closer to 1970s countrypolitan than rock-inflected alt-country, grew more orchestrated over time.

Angel Olsen.summary: Chicago-born-then-Asheville singer whose strange, old-time-adjacent vibrato grew from Bonnie 'Prince' Billy-mentored lo-fi folk into glammy pop-rock, orchestral art-pop and pedal-steel country.

Angela Autumn.summary: Appalachian-raised clawhammer banjo player nicknamed 'The Rose of Appalachia' who folds old-time and bluegrass roots into an arena-sized, psychedelic gothic-country sound.

Angst.summary: San Francisco SST band whose clean, politically engaged folk-punk songwriting stood out as more melodic than the label's noisier hardcore roster.

Anna St. Louis.summary: Los Angeles songwriter whose stark debut opened into brighter, orchestral arrangements on a record made within the overlapping Woodsist singer-songwriter circle.

Anne Briggs.summary: Nottinghamshire folk singer whose plain, unornamented voice and sparse original songs sold poorly but became a hard-to-find cult record among British folk revivalists.

Annie Williams.summary: Nashville debut songwriter whose subtle pop melodies and conversational, funny writing favor wit and understatement, part of the Nashville indie-folk underground.

Appendix Out.summary: Alasdair Roberts's Glasgow band, signed to Drag City after Roberts gave Will Oldham a demo, plays hushed, fingerpicked Scottish folk-rock in the label's deadpan idiom.

Arbor Labor Union.summary: Athens, Georgia punks turned Dead-worshipping jammers whose fuzzed-out cosmic-country evolved from noisy riff-jamming into cleaner, Allman/Wilburys-style songcraft.

Arbouretum.summary: Baltimore band led by Dave Heumann's plainspoken baritone through slow, heavy, extended-jam guitar folk-rock in an explicitly Crazy Horse-scale mode.

Archers of Loaf.summary: Eric Bachmann's Chapel Hill band whose tangled, feedback-streaked guitar interplay and yelped vocals made them instant peers of Pavement and a cornerstone of the scene.

Arlo McKinley.summary: Cincinnati songwriter, personally signed by John Prine to Oh Boy Records, whose weathered voice carries bleak Midwestern country-folk about addiction and hometown decay.

Arthur Alexander.summary: Muscle Shoals soul singer whose early singles were covered by the Beatles, Stones and Dylan, returning here with a warm, country-soul comeback record.

Astrachan.summary: Chicago songwriter Ben Astrachan's maximalist solo debut packs '60s-and-'70s-indebted melodic twists into off-kilter, conceptual guitar-pop.

Austin Lucas.summary: Punk-rooted Bloomington, Indiana songwriter whose plainspoken alt-country grew fuller and more country-radio-adjacent as he moved from Suburban Home to New West Records.

Avett Brothers.summary: Rick Rubin-produced Concord, NC brothers band that smoothed its punk-folk roughness into string-and-piano Americana built for festival-crowd singalongs.

A\u00efda Mekonnen Caby.summary: TOLEDO member's solo turn into pristine, dreamy folk-pop at a more intimate, personal scale than her main band.

B.W. Stevenson.summary: Dallas-based singer from the Austin cosmic-cowboy circle whose big, husky voice pushed progressive country toward pop-crossover hits.

Babehoven.summary: Maya Bon's Hudson Valley project moved from lo-fi duo beginnings into full-band indie folk-pop with country and Americana touches and soaring vocals.

Bad Brains.summary: Washington D.C. jazz-trained musicians who played hardcore at breakneck, technically dazzling speed with reggae interludes, setting the standard for early-80s American hardcore.

Bad Livers.summary: Austin trio, produced by Butthole Surfers' Paul Leary, who ran bluegrass instrumentation at punk speed and volume behind Danny Barnes's deadpan banjo songwriting.

Badfinger.summary: Swansea band on the Beatles' own Apple label whose crisp, chiming, unabashedly Beatlesque songwriting made the Beatles-to-power-pop lineage nearly literal.

Bailter Space.summary: Christchurch band formed by two ex-members of the Gordons who traded the Dunedin sound's chime for churning, noise-caked, motorik guitar rock.

Band of Horses.summary: Ben Bridwell's post-Carissa's Wierd band built big, reverb-soaked, Crazy-Horse-and-My-Morning-Jacket-indebted choruses that grew warmer, more Southern and more polished over time.

Baptist Generals.summary: Chris Flemmons's Denton, Texas band made a scrappy, tape-worn Sub Pop debut of cracked-voice folk-rock within the North Texas DIY scene around Midlake.

Beach Bunny.summary: Lili Trifilio's Chicago project turned bright, hooky power-pop about body image and self-doubt from a viral bedroom EP into arena-ready choruses.

Beachwood Sparks.summary: Los Angeles Paisley Underground pioneers whose pedal-steel-laced, Gram Parsons-descended cosmic country rock anticipated the 2000s revival before returning to it themselves.

Beat Happening.summary: Calvin Johnson, Heather Lewis and Bret Lunsford's deliberately amateurish, home-taped Olympia trio founded the whole lo-fi, twee-adjacent K Records aesthetic.

Beck.summary: Los Angeles songwriter whose home-taped acoustic-blues and tape-collage detours, made with and around Calvin Johnson, aligned him directly with the K Records lo-fi aesthetic.

Bedhead.summary: Dallas twin-brother-led five-piece whose interlocking clean-toned guitars build slowly toward controlled swells over flat, whispered deadpan vocals, a touchstone of guitar-interplay slowcore.

Beirut.summary: Zach Condon's teenage Balkan-brass project, built on ukulele, mandolin and rotating horns, set the template for chamber indie.

Bella White.summary: Calgary-born, bluegrass-trained singer whose Appalachian-rooted picking widens into country, indie and classic-rock textures without losing its traditional core.

Ben Seretan.summary: New York songwriter whose chaotic, ecstatic, hymnlike full-band record swings between grief and communal joy within a prolific DIY solo catalog.

Bert Jansch.summary: London fingerstyle guitarist whose harder-edged folk-blues-jazz playing shaped a generation of British guitarists and directly seeded Pentangle.

Beulah.summary: Elephant 6-affiliated San Francisco band whose fuzzy guitar pop, stray horns and loose, sunny-then-bittersweet arrangements traded on scrappy, homemade psych-pop melody.

Beyonc\u00e9.summary: Pop superstar whose sprawling, star-studded reckoning with country music's Black roots mixes pedal steel and banjo with hip-hop and R&B production.
Beyonc\u00e9.related: Dolly Parton; Willie Nelson; Linda Martell

Big Black.summary: Steve Albini's Chicago project paired a programmed drum machine with clanging, treated guitars and confrontational lyrics to define mechanical, abrasive noise rock.

Big Dipper.summary: Boston band assembled from Volcano Suns and Dumptruck whose hooky, deceptively simple power pop dressed odd lyrical subjects in equal parts jangle and crunch.

Big Star.summary: Alex Chilton and Chris Bell's Memphis band stacked ringing twelve-string guitars and Beatlesque harmonies into the founding document of jangle and power pop.

Big Thief.summary: Adrianne Lenker-led Brooklyn band whose raw, intimate, vividly storytelling indie folk deepened into sprawling double albums and cosmic, ambient-tinged textures.

Big Vic.summary: Ann Arbor band led by Victoria Rinaldi whose fuzzed-out, noisy indie rock was only retroactively tagged countrygaze for its Wilco- and Silver Jews-tinged Americana touches.

Bill Callahan.summary: Chicago-then-Austin songwriter whose deadpan, aphoristic delivery carried his post-Smog solo work from gospel-inflected looseness through folk austerity to warm, groove-based domestic songwriting.

Bill Fox.summary: Cleveland songwriter who left garage-punk band the Mice for thin, close-mic'd, Beatles-echoing home-cassette solo records before a long disappearance from music.

Bill Monroe.summary: Rosine, Kentucky bandleader whose fast, hard-driven string-band music and keening high-lonesome tenor with the classic Blue Grass Boys lineup invented bluegrass as a genre.

Bill Morrissey.summary: New Hampshire folksinger whose dry, novelistic character studies of blue-collar mill-town life were delivered in a warm, conversational baritone over spare acoustic guitar.

Bill Orcutt.summary: Former Harry Pussy noise-guitarist whose battered four-string acoustic playing tears through blues and American song fragments with a violent, broken-string attack.

Billie Marten.summary: UK singer-songwriter, discovered via YouTube covers, whose hushed, breathy, fingerpicked folk grew fuller and more rhythmically alive across her RCA and Fiction Records albums.

Billy Joe Shaver.summary: Nashville outlaw-country songwriter whose rough, talking-blues voice delivered his own working-class, hard-luck character songs as the definitive versions of tunes others made famous.

Billy Strings.summary: Nashville flatpicker whose blistering guitar runs and jam-band-scaled improvisation over traditional bluegrass drew a younger, festival-jam-scene audience into the genre.

Black Flag.summary: Hermosa Beach band whose Henry Rollins-fronted, self-released hardcore turned suburban California rage into lurching brutality, founding the SST/West Coast hardcore underground.

Blackberry Smoke.summary: Atlanta band whose triple-guitar boogie and pedal steel flourishes carried Southern rock's Skynyrd/Allman lineage into 2010s mainstream and country-radio crossover.

Blackfoot.summary: Jacksonville band whose raspy-voiced, harder-rocking take on Southern rock pushed the genre toward arena hard rock rather than the Allmans' jazzier jamming.

Blaze Foley.summary: Austin outlaw-folk songwriter whose rumbling baritone and wrecked-tender, dark-comic songs, caught on a rough club tape shortly before his death, built his posthumous legend.

Blitzen Trapper.summary: Portland band led by Eric Earley's reedy voice through ramshackle folk-rock, Dylan-esque narrative songwriting and classic-rock and prog-inflected detours.

Blood Oranges.summary: Boston band working the country-punk seam a few years ahead of the No Depression name, pairing mandolin and harmony vocals over plainspoken, unhurried songs of hard luck.

Blood on the Saddle.summary: Los Angeles cowpunk band, inspired directly by seeing the Gun Club live, fronted by dual vocalists over fast, rowdy Delta-blues-meets-punk guitar and fiddle.

Bloomsday.summary: Iris James Garrison's spacious, full-bodied New York folk project, recorded at Babehoven's studio with earworm melodies and a wide cast of hushed-folk collaborators.

Blue County Pistol.summary: Rollicking, banjo-heavy alt-country EP act from the small self-released Bandcamp alt-country underground.

Blue Mountain.summary: Oxford, Mississippi band mixing Skynyrd-style twin-guitar boogie with plainspoken insurgent-country storytelling, road-tested like a bar band.

Blue Ranger.summary: New York band bridging electronica, soft-folk and ambient rock, its rustic, anxious songs built slowly around violin textures toward sudden releases.

Bluetile Lounge.summary: Perth, Australia trio recorded in a reverberant Masonic hall, pairing slow, feedback-laced guitar drift with hushed vocals in a rare non-American slowcore entry.

Bnny.summary: Jess Viscius's Chicago project turned grief into inky, minimalist noir-pop with Velvet Underground-simple chords, later fleshing out into fuller slowcore/shoegaze arrangements.

Bob Dylan.summary: New York folk-turned-rock songwriter whose evolution from Guthrie-indebted interpreter to electric literary lyricist to Nashville-crooning country convert reshaped what a song could hold across six decades.

Bob Dylan and The Band.summary: Basement-tape and arena-reunion collaboration between Dylan and his backing group, its loose, homemade Americana and triumphant live reworkings becoming founding texts of roots rock.

Bob Seger.summary: Detroit bar-band rocker whose nostalgic, plainspoken heartland-rock ballads about growing up in Michigan became classic-rock radio standards.

Bob Weir.summary: Grateful Dead guitarist whose solo album, performed almost entirely by his own band, introduced Weir/Barlow songs that immediately became permanent Dead concert staples.

Bob Wills & His Texas Playboys.summary: Tulsa bandleader whose horn-and-fiddle Western swing, broadcast from Cain's Ballroom, established the pedal steel as a lead country instrument.

Bobbie Gentry.summary: Chickasaw County, Mississippi songwriter whose low, unhurried alto and orchestrated Southern gothic story-songs turned Delta gossip into concept-album narrative craft.

Bobby Bare.summary: Nashville baritone whose outlaw-era albums, largely written by Shel Silverstein, treated country songwriting as folklore and dark comic storytelling.

Bobby Bare Jr..summary: Son of outlaw star Bobby Bare Sr. who channeled that lineage into stranger, fuzzed-out, deadpan Nashville-outsider storytelling rock on Bloodshot Records.

Bobby Charles.summary: Louisiana swamp-pop songwriter whose warm, unhurried Bearsville record, cut with members of the Band, blended country, Cajun roots and rock.

Bon Iver.summary: Justin Vernon's Wisconsin cabin-recorded project turned isolation and lo-fi falsetto into the modern hushed singer-songwriter template before expanding into fuller, electronically processed arrangements.

Bonnie 'Prince' Billy.summary: Will Oldham's long-running Louisville persona whose plain, deadpan voice carried Drag City country-folk from mortality-fixated dread through duet-based warmth to orchestrated, hymn-adjacent late records.
Bonnie 'Prince' Billy.related: David Berman; Angel Olsen; the Cairo Gang

Bonnie 'Prince' Billy and the Cairo Gang.summary: A pared-back Bonnie 'Prince' Billy collaboration with guitarist Emmett Kelly, stripping arrangements to two guitars and voice.

Bonny Doon.summary: Detroit band pairing Bill Lennox and Bobby Colombo's warm, conversational harmonies over gentle, unhurried country-folk in the Woodsist slacker lineage.

Bonny Light Horseman.summary: Anaïs Mitchell, Eric D. Johnson and Josh Kaufman's folk supergroup reworking traditional British and American ballads into warm, harmony-driven arrangements.

Brad Goodall.summary: Huntington, West Virginia songwriter whose self-produced piano-man records mix Zevon-ish snark and plainspoken confession in the Randy Newman lineage.

Brandi Carlile.summary: Seattle singer whose big-voiced, orchestral folk-rock balladry scaled festival Americana to Grammy-stage, vocally virtuosic size.

Brennan Wedl.summary: Nashville songwriter whose debut, co-produced by Katie Crutchfield and Brad Cook, blends arena-scaled country-rock hooks with swaggering, confessional lyrics.

Brennen Leigh.summary: Nashville songwriter whose bluegrass-picking prairie concept record and Bob Wills-style Western swing collaboration cover the genre's rural-Midwest and dance-hall wings.

Brent Cobb.summary: Ellaville, Georgia songwriter, produced by cousin Dave Cobb, whose warm, front-porch country-soul owes more to J.J. Cale's laid-back groove than to hard honky-tonk.

Bridget St John.summary: London singer-songwriter, patronized by John Peel who founded Dandelion Records for her, whose low, unhurried contralto and plainspoken fingerpicked songs avoided orchestral flourish.

Bright Eyes.summary: Conor Oberst's Omaha project moved from teenage home-taped scrapbooks and quavering confessional lo-fi into fuller, Emmylou Harris-featuring Americana.

Brown Horse.summary: Norwich, UK band whose stark, road-worn alt-country, recorded live, cites Lucinda Williams, Jason Molina and Silver Jews as touchstones.

Bruce Springsteen.summary: Asbury Park bandleader whose widescreen E Street Band arena rock narrowed into a stark, home-recorded, Guthrie-indebted album of murder ballads before returning to stadium scale.

Buck Meek.summary: Big Thief guitarist whose solo records lean looser and more overtly country, built on plain, warm Telecaster twang and an easygoing drawl.

Buck Owens.summary: Bakersfield bandleader whose bright, biting double-Telecaster twang and hard backbeat defined the Bakersfield sound as a rawer alternative to Nashville's countrypolitan records.

Buck Owens and His Buckaroos.summary: Bakersfield band whose bright, fast, treble-forward twin-guitar sound with pedal steel made Owens a genuine pop chart rival and cemented the commercial Bakersfield sound.

Buddy Miller.summary: Nashville session guitarist turned solo artist whose lean, razor-sharp Telecaster honky-tonk records, built around duets with wife Julie Miller, became central to 1990s Americana.

Buffalo Springfield.summary: Los Angeles quintet pairing Stills and Furay's ringing Byrds-indebted folk rock with Neil Young's early songwriting, the shared origin point for Young's solo career, CSNY and Poco.
Buffalo Springfield.related: Neil Young; Stephen Stills; Richie Furay

Buffalo Tom.summary: Boston band whose thick, Dinosaur Jr.-indebted guitar tone, produced early on by J Mascis, carried Bill Janovitz's raw, unpolished voice into direct, emotionally open songwriting.

Built to Spill.summary: Doug Martsch's Boise band built layered, unhurried Neil-Young-indebted guitar interplay into extended, Crazy-Horse-scale songs, from scrappy early jams to a foundational Pacific Northwest indie-rock catalog.

Bullseye.summary: New York quartet's hooky, jangly and twangy power-pop debut, signed to Ever/Never, favors rock and roll swagger over polish.

Butch Hancock.summary: Lubbock, Texas songwriter whose stark, self-released acoustic records supplied much of the material Joe Ely and Jimmie Dale Gilmore made famous under their own names.

Butterglory.summary: Lawrence, Kansas band whose cheaply recorded, fuzzed-out guitar pop and dual half-mumbled vocals brought the town's lo-fi scene into the Merge slacker-rock conversation.

CMAT.summary: Dublin pop singer whose sardonic, oversharing country-pop reframes breakup pain and Irish life as broad, funny, hooky, arena-scaled songs.

Caitlin Cary.summary: Former Whiskeytown fiddler and harmony singer whose solo debut leans into warmer, more melodic alt-country with her fiddle and clear voice up front.

Caitlin Rose.summary: Nashville-outsider singer whose classic countrypolitan production and wry, contemporary songwriting voice drew comparisons to Loretta Lynn and Skeeter Davis.

Calexico.summary: Joey Burns and John Convertino's Tucson project fuses mariachi horns, spaghetti-Western twang and desert-noir atmosphere into widescreen instrumental Americana.

Califone.summary: Tim Rutili's Chicago project after Red Red Meat builds warped, sample-flecked roots-rock around murmured, deadpan vocals and junk-shop percussion.

Camper Van Beethoven.summary: Redlands/San Francisco band whose gleefully genre-agnostic ska, surf, klezmer-fiddle and punk collage matured into more focused, country- and folk-rock-informed songwriting.

Cantuckee.summary: Mark Scott's side project apart from villagerrr, offering hushed, lo-fi, wandering small-town Americana songs.

Cap'n Jazz.summary: Buffalo Grove, Illinois band whose chaotic, yelped, start-stop math-rock riffing invented Midwest emo and scattered members into American Football and Joan of Arc.

Car Seat Headrest.summary: Will Toledo's project turned prolific Bandcamp bedroom pop into classic-rock-scaled narrative rock before detouring into electronic production and back to guitar-driven concept records.

Carissa's Wierd.summary: Mat Brooke and Jenn Ghetto's Seattle band traded slow, quietly strummed, hushed lo-fi songs that seeded Band of Horses and Grand Archives among its members.

Carmen Perry.summary: Remember Sports co-frontperson's solo debut moves from that band's power-pop punk into earthy, understated, subtly twangy songs.

Case Oats.summary: Chicago band led by Casey Gomez Walker, with Spencer Tweedy on drums, delivering assured pedal-steel-and-fiddle character studies from Walker's creative-writing background.

Cash Langdon.summary: Birmingham, Alabama songwriter whose loud, hooky rock, cut live in Muscle Shoals with his band Meadow Dust, channels Summerteeth-era Wilco and Ty Segall's frantic energy.

Casper Skulls.summary: Toronto band whose dual-vocal, college-rock-indebted jangle pop, drawing on Pavement and R.E.M., grew from scrappy EP into fuller, more anthemic arrangements.

Cass McCombs.summary: Itinerant songwriter whose spare, wry, deadpan narrative songs moved from indie-folk jangle through hushed pedal-steel breakthrough to breezy, Dead-adjacent cosmic country-rock.

Casual Technicians.summary: Oregon home-recording project whose sprawling 24-song grab-bag cycles through folk, slacker jangle, country and doom-metal detours in a GBV-indebted kitchen-sink tradition.

Cat Power.summary: Chan Marshall's project set a fragile, wavering voice against slow, spare guitar that never rushed toward resolution, peaking with a hushed sadcore landmark made with Dirty Three.

Caustic Resin.summary: Boise band, closely tied to Built to Spill, whose heavy, fuzzed-out guitar rock and long wah-drenched solos worship Neil Young & Crazy Horse.

Centro-matic.summary: Will Johnson's Denton, Texas band ran fast, fuzzed-out, home-recorded guitar rock from scrappy 1990s lo-fi into fuller, more anthemic Crazy-Horse-tilted country rock.

Centro-matic and South San Gabriel.summary: A double album pairing Will Johnson's loud Centro-matic guitar rock with his quieter South San Gabriel project, showing both halves of his split musical personality.

Chapterhouse.summary: Reading, UK band blending shoegaze guitar fog with dance-influenced rhythms and drum machines, a less guitar-orthodox branch of the scene alongside Ride and Slowdive.

Charles Wesley Godwin.summary: Morgantown, West Virginia songwriter whose full-band, radio-friendly storytelling country is rooted in specific Appalachian coal-country place and family memory.

Charley Crockett.summary: San Benito, Texas songwriter whose busker-rough beginnings refined into a vintage, laconic honky-tonk persona spanning Gulf Coast soul, cinematic countrypolitan and outlaw-revenge concept records.

Charlie Daniels Band.summary: Nashville session player turned bandleader whose Southern rock merges electric slide, banjo and his own fiddle, name-checking the Allmans and Marshall Tucker as genre peers.

Charlie Hill.summary: Nashville songwriter (formerly Chazzy Lake) whose cleaner-toned indie country blends Laurel Canyon songwriting with ample pedal steel.

Charlie Reed.summary: Chicago full band whose delicate, subdued folk-rock swells into strings and pedal steel around themes of love, loss and cyclical anxiety.

Charlie Rich.summary: Nashville pianist whose smoky, soul-and-blues-inflected piano ballads, produced by Billy Sherrill, gave him a late commercial breakthrough after two decades without a defined identity.

Charlotte Cornfield.summary: Canadian drummer-turned-singer-songwriter whose plainspoken, groove-aware folk-rock grew steadily more confident into warm, Tom-Petty-esque road songs.

Chavez.summary: New York band pairing Matt Sweeney and Clay Tarver's tightly harmonized twin-guitar riffs with a muscular, classic-rock scale unusual for Matador's roster.

Cheap Trick.summary: Rockford, Illinois arena-scale power-pop band whose Beatles-indebted hooks and massed guitars made them one of the genre's biggest commercial successes.

Chico States.summary: Joseph Barresi's Maine project makes dusky, encyclopedic, self-tagged 'ANTI-AMERICANA' with pedal steel and scrappy harmonies mixing personal minutiae with travel history.

Chook Race.summary: Melbourne trio whose tightly-recorded, plainspoken jangling guitar pop sits in the same DIY scene as Dick Diver and the Goon Sax.

Chris Bell.summary: Big Star co-founder whose vaulted solo sessions, released after his death, pair delicate acoustic jangle with despairing, confessional lyrics, the missing link to power pop's wounded strain.

Chris Cacavas & Junkyard Love.summary: Green on Red's longtime keyboardist's Steve Wynn-produced solo debut trades that band's desert-noir menace for simpler, plainspoken country-rock.

Chris Cohen.summary: Former Deerhoof and Curtains member whose warped, subdued, Laurel-Canyon-adjacent psychedelic pop stayed hazy and unhurried across a quietly beloved solo catalog.

Chris Forsyth & the Solar Motel Band.summary: Philadelphia guitarist's move from solo-guitar American Primitivism into full-band, jam-length instrumental rock tracing the electric guitar from Garcia to Sonic Youth.

Chris Hillman.summary: Byrds and Flying Burrito Brothers bassist whose direct, unpretentious solo country rock, played by crack LA session musicians, continued his post-Byrds pedigree.

Chris Knight.summary: Rural Kentucky songwriter whose flat, unsentimental songs about hard rural life, guns and addiction, delivered in a plainspoken drawl, anticipated Drive-By Truckers' storytelling.

Chris Knox.summary: Auckland songwriter whose cheap four-track, drum-machine home recordings turned confessional, producing one of the Flying Nun catalog's most beloved songs.

Chris Stamey.summary: Former dB's member whose stranger, more experimental solo debut mixed chiming guitar pop with synths and studio effects on his own label.

Chris Stapleton.summary: Nashville songwriter turned solo artist whose enormous, gravel-and-smoke voice over old-school Southern-rock and soul instrumentation reoriented mainstream country toward rootsier production.

Christmas.summary: Boston band playing jittery, hook-heavy college rock with deadpan, absurdist lyrics riding bright, angular, new-wave-inflected guitars.

Chuck Johnson.summary: Oakland guitarist whose steel-string American Primitive playing pushes toward drone, slide lines bending like raga figures under electronic haze.

Cian Nugent.summary: Dublin guitarist whose long, patient solo pieces on the VHF label draw on both the American Takoma tradition and British folk guitarists like Bert Jansch.

Circle Jerks.summary: Los Angeles hardcore band, formed by an ex-Black Flag singer, whose fourteen-song, fifteen-minute debut of pure speed and sneering humor became an era-defining landmark.

Circles Around the Sun.summary: Neal Casal-formed instrumental jam group, soundtracking a Grateful Dead box set before pushing toward groovier cosmic-disco.

Clem Snide.summary: Eef Barzelay's Boston band built deadpan, pop-culture-strewn lyrics over spare alt-country arrangements closer in spirit to Silver Jews than to Nashville twang.

Clifford.summary: Boston band whose noise-and-jangle swings feature moody slowcore passages with a subtle twang running underneath.

Cocteau Twins.summary: Grangemouth, Scotland band whose Elizabeth Fraser's wordless, glossolalia-like vocals over Robin Guthrie's chiming, reverb-soaked guitar defined the ethereal 4AD dream-pop sound.

Codeine.summary: New York band whose flat, weary baritone over guitars tuned down and dragged to a crawl helped found American slowcore as a named genre.

Cody Jinks.summary: Fort Worth outlaw revivalist whose doom-metal-adjacent guitar heaviness and cavernous baritone gave straight outlaw-country songwriting unusual weight, built entirely outside the major-label system.

Cody Johnson.summary: Sebastopol, Texas dancehall-circuit independent star whose fiddle-and-steel instrumentation stayed intact as his arena-country ambitions scaled up into the Nashville mainstream.

Colin Miller.summary: Asheville engineer behind MJ Lenderman's and Wednesday's records whose own bittersweet, homespun folk-rock draws on shared-memory storytelling from his local scene.

Color Green.summary: Los Angeles quartet whose loose, live-feeling jams and four trading vocalists work a '60s SoCal folk-rock and Dead/Allmans-descended vocabulary.

Colter Wall.summary: Swift Current, Saskatchewan singer whose startlingly deep baritone over spare acoustic and Western-swing arrangements built one of neo-traditional country's strictest classicist personas.

Commander Cody and His Lost Planet Airme.summary: Ann Arbor band relocated to San Francisco mixing western swing, boogie-woogie piano and hot-rod rockabilly into a rowdier, funnier country-rock than the Byrds/Burritos axis.

Connie Smith.summary: Nashville singer whose clear, powerful, honky-tonk-phrased voice on a devastating heartbreak ballad became an instant influence on younger singers including Dolly Parton.

Convinced Friend.summary: A.S. Wilson's Providence project fuses serene twang with apocalyptic indie rock, reflecting on his eroding native Houma, Louisiana coastline.

Conway Twitty.summary: Nashville singer whose whispered, intimate-baritone country hits marked his full transition from rockabilly teen idol to mainstream Nashville hitmaker.

Corb Lund.summary: Alberta ranch-country songwriter whose wry, detail-heavy songs about cattle, rodeo and small-town prairie life, backed by the Hurtin' Albertans, gave alt-country a distinctly Canadian regional voice.

Cordelia's Dad.summary: Northampton, Massachusetts band that turned Anglo-American traditional folk tunes into loud, Dinosaur Jr.-indebted rock, an unheralded forerunner of the No Depression movement.

Cory Branan.summary: Mississippi-raised, Memphis-adjacent songwriter whose wordy, funny-sad, syllable-packed storytelling ranges across punk-speed rockers, piano ballads and pure country weepers.

Cory Chisel.summary: Appleton, Wisconsin songwriter whose warm, reverent Americana blends gospel, soul and folk influences carried by his rich, soulful voice.

Cory Hanson.summary: Wand frontman's solo work stripped fuzzed-out psych down to gentle, pedal-steel-laced Laurel Canyon folk-rock before swinging through long guitar-jam epics and orchestral Nashville Sound balladry.

Cotton Jones.summary: Michael Croll's post-Wooden Wand project makes hazy, softly psychedelic country-folk built around close harmonies with Whitney McGraw.

Country Gazette.summary: Flying Burrito Brothers fiddler Byron Berline's bluegrass band pushed the LA country-rock scene's picking side to its most virtuosic, straight-bluegrass extreme.
